question: A 32-year-old man arrives in the emergency department actively seizing. The seizure has lasted 7 minutes (confirmed by paramedics). IV access is established. According to the stepwise management of convulsive status epilepticus, which drug should be given FIRST and at what stage does this represent?

answers.text: IV phenytoin (or fosphenytoin) — second-line agent, given because the 30-minute threshold has been crossed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Phenytoin is the second-line agent used when benzodiazepines fail (typically after ~10 minutes of ongoing SE), not at 7 minutes. The 30-minute threshold is an older definition of refractory SE.

answers.text: IV lorazepam — first-line benzodiazepine, given because the ≥5-minute operational definition of SE is met

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. SE is operationally defined as a seizure lasting ≥5 minutes. IV lorazepam (0.1 mg/kg, max 4 mg) is the first-line agent when IV access is available. At 7 minutes this patient meets the threshold.

answers.text: IV valproate — first-line agent, preferred because it is non-sedating

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IV valproate is a second-line or third-line agent used when benzodiazepines fail or are contraindicated. Benzodiazepines remain first-line for acute SE.

answers.text: Buccal midazolam — first-line when IV access is already established

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Buccal (or intranasal) midazolam is the preferred route when IV access is NOT available (e.g., in the community). Once IV access is established, IV lorazepam is preferred.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the stepwise approach: SE definition (≥5 min or ≥2 seizures without recovery) → IV lorazepam (or IM/buccal midazolam if no IV) → if failing at ~10 min, add IV phenytoin/valproate/levetiracetam.
Correct. SE threshold = ≥5 min → IV lorazepam first (or buccal midazolam if no IV access).
